Kuṟuntokai 130. Veḷḷi Vīti(yār): the confidante / SHE

lg.l: The speech where [the heroine] divulges [her situation to the confidante] because of [her] excessive love [for the hero];

the speech of the confidante while [the hero] has gone outside the surrounding wall [of the house];In this situation, the heroine’s friend speaks to herself while the hero is within earshot, though not visible, and so, in practice, speaks to him.
[the confidante] informing [the hero] of her confinement; [the confidante] thinking, ‘[The hero has made] a vow’;
[the confidante] speaking about [the heroine’s] death; [the hero expressing] the necessity to come at night;
[the confidante] rejecting [that idea]; [the confidante] agreeing [to the idea]; [the confidante] designating the meeting-place;
[the confidante] speaking so [the heroine] agrees [to the tryst]; [the confidante] informing [the heroine] that he is coming;
[the confidante] leading her to the designated place;
[the confidante] speaking about the false sign along with [the hero] leaving while [the hero] is outside the surrounding wall; [the hero] suffering
– [these] are [the situations of] the nighttime tryst that occurs outside of the house.

div.p: eṉpatu iravuk kuṟi yām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which the nighttime tryst occurs.
vāy viṭu kiḷavi mutal ākat talaimakaṉeñcoṭu nōtal īṟākac collap paṭṭaṉa vil varai yikavā viravuk kuṟi yām eṉṟa vāṟu.
Beginning with ‘the speech [where she] divulges’ and ending with ‘the hero suffering with his heart’, the things mentioned are the nighttime tryst that occurs outside the boundary of the house.

lg.l: Cutting down the soft aṭumpu vines, under the cruel sun,
my heart went after the lord in the tall chariot,
who had come to the winding backwaters and departed.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ āṟṟāmaik kaṇ vāy viṭu kiḷavi.
This is the speech where the heroine divulges her inability to bear [her current situation].

lg.l: O red-beaked swan, if you and your mate
were to scold the lord with a spear in his hand,
would there be anything to gain? Tell us!

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Because the lord of choice rays joined the road,There are two potential interpretations for how this could refer to sunset, which it does: either the sun joins with the road in the sense that it meets where the road crosses the horizon, thereby setting, or it joins with its path, i.e., it goes along its prescribed route, thereby setting.
didn’t the large flocks of birds separate and leaveThe interrogative value of -mātō is not clear. Is the confidante simply wondering to herself out loud? It is not clear what it brings to the poem.
so that she, with a heart full of pain, suffered?

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ ciṟaip puṟam ākap piṟitiṉ mēl vaittut tōḻi kūṟiyatu.
This is the confidante having spoken [about the heroine’s suffering], blaming it on something else, while the hero is behind the wall.

lg.l: O spotless moon, do you have a lover,
who unites in the evening and leaves in the morning?
When it is night, you are good, [but] in the day,
you are even dimmer than the forehead
of the vine[-like] lady with the soft nature.

div.p: ituvum atu.
And this is that.

lg.l: Mother, may she live,vāḻi here seems to simply function like an expletive. It is not obviously attached to any addressee, unlike in other formulaic occurrences. yesterday looked sweetly
at the young girl’s budding breasts with their soft nature

and then back at me again and again.pal muṟai could theoretically mean ‘in many ways’, but as the idea of the poem is that the mother is coming to a realisation about her daughter’s maturity, this repetition makes more sense.

div.p: eṉpatu kuṟippiṉāṟ ceṟippaṟivuṟuttatu.
This is [the confidante] indirectly having informed [the hero] about [the heroine’s] confinement.

lg.l: Because he was one who became intimate [with her] and brought sweet words,tarunariṉ is understood as a fifth case in this translation, but the form is morphologically ambiguous. It could also be construed as a genitive, in which case: ‘What should I say about the thoughts of separation from here of him who, having become close [to her], brought sweet words?’

what shall I say about [his] thoughtcūḻntaṉṟu is analysed as a neuter singular participial noun – ‘the thing thought about’. It can just as well be a perfective finite neuter singular, but that would require supplying a subject. The root is transitive, so it cannot be that the separation ‘was devised by the one who…’ One could take an impersonal subject: ‘there was the planning of separation by…’ This is possible and would require the following interrogative phrase to be its own sentence. of separation from here?īṅku could also mean ‘such’. One could also make a different wordsplit: tarunariṉ nīṅkup pirivu, which would mean ‘the leaving separation’.

That is the job of the kino tree.The confidante is expressing her disapproval at his separation, and she names the kino tree, which invokes thoughts of marriage, to suggest to him the appropriate course of action.

div.p: eṉpatu ciṟaip puṟattuc ceṟippaṟivuṟuttatu.
This is [the confidante] having informed [the hero] about [the heroine’s] confinement while he was behind the wall.

lg.l: O lord, tell [us] what should rightfully be done!I follow the PK (see the critical notes to this poem) in interpreting the first line. At a stretch, this could be an exhortation on the part of the confidante for the hero to jump into action: ‘Speak, O Lord! The thing to be done is rightfully [yours]’ (i.e., ‘You should take action’).
As the kino tree expands its fragrant buds,The kino tree flowering marks the harvest season, at which point the lovers lose their cover as they used to meet in the millet field.

after the ears drooped, the millet in our harvest field has perished.I was not sure how to construe this line. oḻintatu ought to be the predicate, in which case the subject should be a singular. This rules out kuṟal (‘the ears of crop’), leaving tiṉai (‘millet’), which is a mass noun referring to the crop as a whole. This works, but then there is no subject-coherence between the viṉaiyeccam and the predicate.

div.p: eṉpatu veḷip paṭac ceṟippaṟivuṟuttatu.
This is [the confidante] having clearly informed [the hero] about [the heroine’s] confinement.

lg.l: If there is falsehood in youIn this translation, vāy is understood as a locative postposition, but one could also take it as a noun meaning ‘mouth’, in which case the phrase would mean: ‘If there were lies in/from your mouth’. In practice, the two mean essentially the same thing. The poem is translated as is because it is modelled after PK 161, where falsehood appears in the hero – poyyoṉṟu niṉkaṇ nikaḻum. concerning the girlAlternatively: ‘did you lie to the girl…’. The idea in the poem seems to be that the hero has lied about the girl rather than to her, hence the translation presented, but the alternative does also make some sense.
with the choice jewels and the pretty soft grace,
who else will speak the truth?

div.p: eṉpatu cūḷ eṉa niṉaintatu.
This is [the confidante] having thought, ‘[The hero made] a vow’.

lg.l: O man from the land with the slopes,

where there are jackfruit trees with bunches of fruitThis translation of vēr kōḷ palaviṉ follows UVC’s gloss. The other option is: ‘Jackfruit trees that take to their roots’, i.e., they bend down under the weight of their fruit. behind bamboo fences,

do the right thing!cevviyai ākumati literally translates to: ‘become [the one who acts] at the right time.’ As the context is that the confidante is urging the hero to marry the heroine, ‘do the right thing’ expresses this in natural English. Who knows [her state of mind]?
Like the large jackfruits hanging from small branches on the slope,
Oh, her life is small but her desire is great.

div.p: eṉpatu āṟṟāḷ eṉpatu paṭak kūṟiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having told how she cannot bear [this situation].

lg.l: O bright-clustered kino tree! O bright-clustered kino tree!
O kino tree, free from branches that do not rejoice with kin,This is opaque. Is it somehow a way to say the branches are flowering and that there are no longer any birds on them?
chasing away the sound “Ayō!”This is the sound lovers make to chase away parakeets from their trysting-place. from that place.

div.p: eṉpatu eṉa varuvaṉavuṅ koḷka.
Understand [others] also come like this.eṉa varuvaṉavum koḷka is a phrase found in commentaries to indicate other such examples exist, but are not cited here (cf. end of commentary to TPn 197).

lg.l: If you were to say, ‘We will separate,’

leavingIt makes no difference to the meaning of the poem, but the infinitive phrase in the first line could also be included in the speech to the heart. the girl with rows of banglesOr, understanding vari as ‘line, stripe’: ‘the girl with striped bangles…’. on her arms all alone.
Don’t become so desolate and grieve! Live, O heart!

Reaching her atThis translation takes iṭai as a locative postposition, but it needn’t be. One could also understand its independent meaning ‘middle’, in which case: ‘the middle of the night’. night is stillHow exactly to take the -āl particle? It can either function as a semantically empty marker of the finite verb, or as an assertive particle. I translate the latter here. attainable for us.

div.p: eṉpatu iruḷ vara vēṇṭal.
This is [the hero expressing] the necessity to come at night.

lg.l: O lord with the rowsnirai could either refer to the hero wearing multiple garlands, or a garland (or multiple ones) arranged in a specific way. of garlands!One could construe niraitār aṇṇal differently, and take it as the cause for the bamboo to drop its pearls. Its initial position in the poem, however, suggests a vocative. If the cause, then one would have to account for why he would make the bamboo drop pearls. Contextually, it makes sense the confidante would warn him of an unrelated context that would make his journey in the night difficult. If the danger derived from something he could change with his actions, one imagines the focus of the poem would be different. Other such examples focus on the threat from wild animals and the like – all things outside of his control.
Because of the spreading of the pearls of expanding rays,
which are dropped from the tall bamboo,This is one of the eight sources of pearls in old South Asian literature (Hara 1999, 156).
night too will indeed shine like day here.

div.p: eṉpatu iraviṉ varutal ariteṉṟatu.
This is [the confidante] having said [to the hero], ‘Coming at night is difficult.’

lg.l: He is not inappropriateLiterally, nēr means ‘to be appropriate’. The idea here is that the hero normally possesses a sort of clarity of mind and acts in a righteous, upstanding way. – the man of great perception.
He has not transgressed. He possesses a great love.

[And yet,] your lordiṉaiyōṉ iṉaiyaṉ is another potential split. This would amount to the same general meaning, but expressed differently: ‘such a man (the lord) has become such a man’. has become such a manSuch a man who asks for a tryst. The idea is that no one in their right mind would do something so risky and desperate, yet because he is lovesick, he has become desperate.
because he cannot bear [not meeting] and has lost his self-control.

div.p: eṉpatu nērtal.
This is [the confidante] agreeing [to his nighttime visit].

lg.l: The fragrance-emitting sandal, that’s our sandal.

And the flower is the glory lily, full of the weight [of its bloom].poṟai mali kāntaḷ is ambiguous. One option is to take poṟai as ‘hillock’, in which case the flowers would be abundant on the hill. The sources and parallels for these poems suggest another reading. In the PK (see apparatus), the only location mentioned in the poem is the grove that the presented translation follows. The Cilappatikāram phrase more closely resembles the one found here, and there the implication is clearly that the flower is carrying the weight of its blossoms, i.e., it is in full bloom.
The aśoka grove where winged bees buzz is [our] playground.

div.p: eṉpatu iravuk kuṟi yiṭaṅ kūṟiṟṟu.
This is [the confidante] having indicated the place for the nighttime tryst.

lg.l: The man from the slopesThe -um on cilampaṉum is not clear. There is nothing for it to co-ordinate with and cilampaṉ must be the subject of the masculine singular verb, arukiṉaṉ. Maybe something like ‘also’ or ‘already’, in which case: ‘The man from the slopes… has also/already made clear…’. of the great mountain, tall from a distance,
where pure white waterfalls resound like drums
on the mountainside of dense bamboo thickets and broad rocks,

has also made his intentionsarukiṉaṉ can also mean ‘to approach’. In that case the confidante would be telling her that he is already nearby, or that he is approaching them again. In either case, this could persuade the heroine to accept the tryst as his proximity increases the chance of them being found out. very clear towards the girl with the bright forehead.

div.p: eṉpatu iravuk kuṟi nayappittatu.
This is [the confidante] having encouraged [the heroine] to accept [the invitation to] the nighttime tryst.

lg.l: Aren’t we ashamed of reproach,vaṭu can also mean ‘injury’ or ‘blemish’. The basic idea is the same with all translations. The girls are either afraid of their own reproach (as in, reproach directed at them), were he to be hurt on the dangerous route to see them, or afraid of the metaphorical blemish on them that would be his dangerous journey. O friend,
that would come with the arrival at midnight
to the difficult-to-reach grove, where the old antagonism
of the small-eyed elephant attacking the tiger languishes,
of the man from the land with the tall mountains and resounding white waterfalls?

div.p: eṉpatu maṟuttatu.
This is [the heroine] having refused [the hero’s invitation].

lg.l: After escaping the murder as the strong tiger with curved stripes attacked
and crossing the difficult desert at deepest midnight,
it is the duty of the girl with the heavy earrings

to open the door at least a littleyāvatum is slightly ambiguous. I construe it with the verb, but one could theoretically also take it with kataṉ (‘duty’). Its semantic weight is also ambiguous. It can mean ‘at all’, ‘a little’, ‘in any way’, ‘anything’. Many of these options seem fitting in either syntactic construction, with no clear way to judge one better than the other. I have simply chosen the one that felt most natural to me, but I do not feel confident it is the correct interpretation. for the one who has come to our abode.

div.p: eṉpatu valitākac colli nayappittatu.
This is [the confidante] having encouraged [the heroine] to accept [the hero’s invitation] by speaking forcefully.

lg.l: The birds have left their resting place
and the sapphire-colouredmaṇi can either convey that the fruit are sapphire-coloured, or that they are gem-sized. fruit of the mastwood tree
full of petals falls in the flood.

I quickly thought of the lord of fierce power.ṉiṉaintaṉaṉ viraintu is open to other interpretations. For one, it can either be a masculine or first person singular. I opt for the first person as otherwise the relation between the absolutive and finite verb is unclear. As a first person, the confidante sees the signs of the hero’s arrival and she quickly realises it is the hero coming. If the hero is the subject of the verb, then she sees the signs and implies that he is coming by saying, ‘he thinks [of us]’. How then would one understand viraintu? It could be that he ‘urgently thinks [of them]’, though that seems like a slightly odd conclusion for her to reach. The other option is to understand it as a prior action, but once again, that doesn’t quite make sense. It is the inverse of what one would expect – for him to think of the heroine and then hurry.

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi varavuṇarntatu.
This is the confidante having realised that [the hero is] coming.

lg.l: ‘Mother! Mother! Look!’aṉṉāy could alternatively be the form of address that the confidante sometimes uses for the heroine. In that case, she is waking her up to let her know the hero has come and that her mother is asleep so the path is clear. The koḷu to TK 161 suggests this interpretation: tāyatuyilaṟin tāytarukiṉṟa mētakutōḻi melliyaṟkicattatu. The presented translation is supported by the AN parallel (see apparatus). Saying this twice,
even though I tried to wake her, she slept.

AndThe meaning of the -um particle on aṇṇalum is not clear. Is this co-ordinating with the verb maṭi-tal, as I have translated? Otherwise, a sense of emphasis would be appropriate, but that is not a commonly accepted meaning for the particle (see TC 257n). his majesty with the long spear with a shining leaf-tip
has come to the meeting-place to make our lonely misery go away.

div.p: eṉpatu varavuṇarttiyatu.
This is [the confidante] having informed [the heroine] that [the hero is] coming.

lg.l: O [one with] a garland dripping nectar!kaḷ aviḻ kōtai does not need to be a vocative. The confidante could be suggesting that they go to pick flowers for a garland.
Let us pick water lilies that are like your eyes

and jasmine buds that are like your sharp teethmuḷ eyiṟṟu literally translates to ‘thorn teeth’, but as the associations attached to something thorny are negative in English, it was not used. in the cool grove.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉ varavuṇarntu tōḻi talaimakaḷaik kuṟi vayiṉ uyttatu.
This is the confidante having led the heroine to the designated place after realising that the hero is coming.

lg.l: If you have seen the blue water lilies,
O one with the grace of a peacock’s feathers and koel-like speech,
after joining me to look at these things over here,

you should do me the grace of returning [with me].Whether or not to take peyarntaṉai aruḷal as a muṟṟeccam is not clear. If so: ‘It is necessary to return and be gracious’, or something similar. This translation diverts from the syntax of the Tamil as there is a natural English phrase that expresses the idea.

div.p: eṉpatu koṇṭu nīṅkal.
This is [the confidante] taking [the heroine] and leaving.

lg.l: O young woman with the aimpāl in waves and curls and a bright forehead,
he doesn’t know how to join us.

The groups of birds all totally forgot to sleep a wink.puṇar is understood as ‘in unison’, i.e., ‘all’, yāvatum as ‘even a little’, colloquially ‘a wink’ in relation to sleep, and peritu as ‘in a big way’, i.e., ‘totally’.

div.p: eṉpatu alla kuṟip paṭutal ciṟaip puṟam ākac colliṟṟu.
This is [the confidante] having spoken about the occurrence of a false sign while [the hero] is behind the wall.

lg.l: O heart who yearns for something difficult [to obtain],
thinking of the girl whose bamboo-like arms have rows of bangles,
it is your fate to obtain great affliction as well.Presumably in addition to obtaining union with the heroine. Otherwise it is not clear what the function of the -um particle is.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaṉeñcoṭu nontatu. 18.
This is the hero having suffered with his heart.

standOff.note: Cf. TP133n: allakuṟip paṭutalu mavaḷvayi ṉurittē | yavaṉkuṟi mayaṅkiya vamaivoṭu variṉē ||
Cf. IA17: allakuṟip paṭutalu mavvayi ṉurittē | yavaṉvara vaṟiyuṅ kuṟippi ṉāṉa ||
Cf. TP131n: iravuk kuṟiyē yillakat tuḷḷu | maṉaiyōr kiḷavi kēṭkumvaḻi yatuvē | maṉaiyakam pukāak kālai yāṉa ||
Cf. IA19: iravuk kuṟiyē yilvarai yikavātu ||
TP 130n and IA 18, which were provided as sources for the previous cūttiram, should be considered as sources for this one as well. They state that a tryst can occur in both the daytime and nighttime.
Cf. IAC18, p. 141: uṭaṉāyirunta puḷḷunōkki ivai kaṇṭu āṟṟic celvāṭku ivaiyum nīṅkiṉa, iṉi eṅṅaṉam aṟṟuṅkollōveṉat talaimakaṟkucciṟaippuṟaṉākaccollum.
Cf. IAC18, p. 142: iṉit, tōḻi varaivukaṭāvuvakai kuṟippiṉāṉ varaivukaṭāvutal
Cf. IAC18, p. 142: kuṟippiṉāṉ varaivukaṭāvumāṟu: yāy em uṟuppiṟ kuṟikkoṇṭu nōkkiṉāḷeṉṉum.
Cf. IAC18, p. 142: iṉit tōḻi varaivukaṭāvuvakai… veḷippaṭaiyāṉ varaivukaṭāvutal

Cf. IAC18, p. 143: iṉi ivviṭattu varappeṟām eṉpatupaṭat talaimakaṟkut tōḻi muṉṉiṉṟu collavumpeṟum. iṉi muṉṉilaippuṟamoḻiyākat talaimakaṉatu varavu uṇarntu vēṅkaikku uraippāḷāyt talaimakaṉkēṭpa ivvāṟu colliyuñ ceṟippaṟivuṟuttum.
Cf. IAC18, p. 144: tōḻi cūḷuṟavākak karutiṉāḷ.
Cf. IAC18, p. 146: iṉit teruḷāṉāyiṉ iravukkuṟivārā varaivaleṉṉum.
Cf. AV158.1: iṟaiyōṉ yiruṭkuṟi vēṇṭal
Though the C1 reading makes sense, Cām corresponds to the phrase found in the cūttiram in line 4.
Cf. AV158.1–2: pāṅki | neṟiyiṉa tarumai kūṟal
Cf. IAC18, p. 146: āṟṟāṉāyiṉ iṟantupaṭumeṉak karuti, iṟantupāṭṭu accattiṉāṉ iravukkuṟi nērum.
Cf. AV157.1: uṭaṉpaṭal
Cf. AV158.5–6: avaṟkut | taṉṉāṭ ṭaṇiyiyal pāṅki cāṟṟal

The AV considers this a precursor to the hero setting the place for the tryst. As Takahashi suggests, the three speech situations enumerated in AV 158.4–7 correspond to this situation (Takahashi 1995, 128, fn. 78). The one provided is the most close parallel.

Cf. IAC18, p. 146: yaṅṅaṉam maṟukkumōveṉiṉ aravum urumum puliyum eṇkum veṇkōṭṭiyāṉaiyumeṉṟu ivaṟṟatu ētam uṭaittu; ēṟṟiḻivuṭaittāya aruvarai yiṭattu oruvēl tuṇaiyāka nīyir āriruḷ naṭunāḷ varavu āṟṟu nīrmaiyavōveṉṉum.
Cf. AV157.1: maṟuttal
Cf. AV158.11–12: kuṟiyiṭai niṟīit tāytuyi laṟitalu | miṟaivik kiṟaivaṉ varavaṟi vuṟuttal
The AV expands on what one finds in the TNV, where the content of the poem aligns with the first AV situation cited directly above as a parallel, and the koḷu with the second.
Cf. AV158.13: avaṭkoṇṭu cēṟal
Cf. IAC18, p. 148: puṇarcciyiṟutikkaṇ tōḻi talaimakaḷaik koṇṭupōtum.
Cf. AV158.13: kuṟiyuyt takaṟal
Cf. AV160.7: iṟaivaṉmēṟ pāṅki kuṟipiḻaip pēṟṟal
Cf. AN80.8–10: oṇpaṇ malarak kavaṭṭilai yaṭumpiṉ | ceṅkēḻ meṉkoṭi yāḻi yaṟuppa | viṉamaṇip paravi neṭuntēr kaṭaii
Cf. PK147.3–4 (IAC18, p. 140): arumā maṇitikaḻ kāṉaliṉ vāyvan takaṉṟakoṇkaṉ | ṟirumā maṇineṭun tēroṭu ceṉṟateṉ cintaṉaiyē ||
One expects assimilation without elision when word-final -ṉ of a monosyllabic word with a short vowel is followed by n-, so in this case eṉ + neñcē = eṉ ṉeñcē.
Cf. IAC18, p. 140: āṟṟaḷāy neñcu mikkatu vāycōrntu kaṭaliṟkāṉuṅ, kāṉaliṟkāṉum, puḷḷiṟkāṉum, neñciṟkāṉum vaṟitē kuḻavi aḻutāṟpōla yātāṉum oru coṟ collum.

Cf. PK148 (IAC18, p. 141): aṉṉam puraiyu naṭaiyāḷ pulampeyta vattameṉṉum | poṉṉañ cilampu katirōṉ maṟaitalum pōyiṉavāṟ | ṟeṉṉaṉ ṟirumāl kaḻaṉeṭu māṟaṉ ṟiruntuceṅkōṉ | maṉṉaṉ kumarik karuṅkaḻi mēyntavaṇ ṭāṉaṅkaḷē ||
Cf. PK149.3–4 (IAC18, p. 141): karuṅkaḻi mēyntaceṅ kālveḷḷai yaṉṉaṅ katiroṭuntam | peruṅkaḻi kātaṉmai nīṅki yivaṉiṟ pirintaṉavē ||

Cf. PK150 (IAC18, p. 141): mēyiṉa tampaṭai yōṭumem melliya lāḷaiventīp | pāyiṉa mālaikkuk kāṭṭik koṭuttup parantumaṇmē | lāyiṉa cīrari kēcarik kaṉṟaḷa nāṭṭuṭaintu | pōyiṉa tevvariṟ pōyiṉa kāṉaliṟ puḷḷiṉamē ||

Cf. AN150.1–6: piṉṉuviṭa neṟitta kūntalum poṉṉē | vākat tarumpiya taṇaṅkum vampuviṭak | kaṇṇurut teḻutaru mulaiyu nōkki | yelliṉai periteṉap paṉmāṇ kūṟip | peruntō ḷaṭaiya muyaṅki nīṭuniṉain | taruṅkaṭip paṭuttaṉaḷ yāyē
Cf. PK152.3–4 (IAC18, p. 143): ākattu vantarumpu | miḷamulai nōkkiniṉ ṟeṉṉaiyu nōkkiṉa ḷemmaṉaiyē ||
Cf. TK132.3–4: kaṉittoṇṭai vāycci katirmulaip pārippuk kaṇṭaḻivuṟ | ṟiṉikkaṇ ṭilampaṟṟuc ciṟṟiṭaik keṉṟañcu memmaṉaiyē ||

The C1 reading yāṅkeṉa (yāṅku eṉa) can also make sense: ‘Because, having become close to her, he brought sweet words, shall I [now] say, “what about [his] thoughts of leaving from here?”’ However, the specific form moḻikō, in the old corpus, when used with an interrogative, is always used in the context of a question meaning ‘What shall I say?’ Thus, I follow UVC’s emendation, which provides this meaning.
Cf. PK153.1 (IAC18, p. 143): ceyaṉmaṉṉu māvatu collāy cilampa
Cf. TK141.3–4: naṉaikeṭac ceytaṉa māyi ṉamaikkeṭac ceytiṭuvāṉ | tiṉaikeṭac ceytiṭu māṟumuṇ ṭōvit tirukkaṇiyē ||

The TK poem is not the most direct parallel, but it deals with the same general topos – the kino tree flowering marks the time for harvest, which means the lovers can no longer meet amongst the millet in the day.
Cf. AN286.15–17 (IAC18, p. 145): nammō raṉṉōr māṭṭu miṉṉa | poyyoṭu miṭaintavai tōṉṟiṉ | meyyāṇ ṭuḷatōviv vulakat tāṉē ||

Cf. PK161 (IAC18, p. 145): neyyoṉṟu vēṉeṭu māṟaṉṟeṉ ṉāṭaṉṉa nēriḻaiyim | maiyoṉṟu vāṭkaṇ maṭantai tiṟattiṭ ṭaṟantirintu | poyyoṉṟu niṉkaṇ ṇikaḻumeṉ ṟāṟpiṉṉaip pūñcilampā | meyyoṉṟu miṉṟi yoḻiyuṅkol lōviv viyaliṭamē ||
Cf. PK162.2–4 (IAC18, p. 145): vaiyai yaṉṉā ṭiṟattuvaṇṭār | viraippā ṉaṟuṅkaṇṇi yāypoymmai nīcolliṉ meymmaiyeṉpa | turaippār piṟariṉi yāvarkol lōviv vulakiṉuḷḷē ||

The poem both reads better with UVC’s emendation to the non-past participial noun and more closely resembles its source material, which I believe the poet was consciously echoing. The C1 reading is a participial noun formed from the past stem, and with that reading one loses the thrust of the final rhetorical question – ‘Who else will speak the truth?’ We also find the exact same morpho-syntactic structure in the fifth example poem of TNV 16 – yārō teḷikkunar piṟarē – that poses the exact same type of question. The corresponding phrase in PK 162 also poses this question in the non-past: uraippār piṟar iṉi yāvarkollō (‘now who will speak [the truth]?’).
Cf. PK155.3–4 (IAC18, p. 143): varaiyār tiṉaippuṉaṅ kālkoyya naṉṉāḷ varaintuniṉṟa | viraiyār malariyal vēṅkāy niṉakku viṭaiyillaiyē ||

Unless UVC misread nē in C1 for tē – a possibility, albeit a very unlikely one – he may have emended to tēraṉ as it is closer in meaning to pēruṇarviṉaṉ and thus, with the negative allaṉ, makes for a clearer juxtaposition. However, a similar effect is achieved by retaining the C1 reading.
Cf. Cilap7, Kānalvari, 8.2: poṟaimalipūmpuṉṉaip pūvutirntu nuṇṭātu pōrkkuṅkāṉal
Cf. PK163.3–4 (IAC18, p. 147): cantaṉañ cāntuceṅ kāntaḷam pūttaḻal pōlviriyuṅ | kontaṇaṅ kīrmpiṇṭi yāmviḷai yāṭuṅ kuḷirpoḻilē ||
Cf. PK164.3–4 (IAC18, p. 147): cantameñ cāntam viḷaiyā ṭiṭamun taḷaiyaviḻum | pūntaḷam piṇṭi yeripōl viriyum poḻilakamē ||
Cf. IAC18, p. 146: eṉṟakkāl tōḻiyāṅ kāntaḷum vēṅkaiyuñ cūṭutuñ cantaṉamuñ cāntum pūcutum, piṇṭi marattiṉkīḻ viḷaiyāṭuva teṉṉum.
Cf. TK154.2–4: poli cāntaṇintu | cuṉaivaḷar kāvikaḷ cūṭip paintōkai tuyilpayiluñ | ciṉaivaḷar vēṅkaikaḷ yāṅkaṇiṉ ṟāṭuñ ceḻumpoḻilē ||
Because of the similarities to the IAC prose passage quoted and PK 163, where the grove is described as the heroine’s playground, the emendation by UVC is retained.
Cf. KT78.1–3: peruvarai micaiyatu neṭuveḷ ḷaruvi | mutuvāyk kōṭiyar muḻaviṟ ṟatumpic | cilampi ṉiḻitaru milaṅkumalai veṟpa
Cf. TK157.3–4: muḻaṅkā rarimuraṇ vāraṇa vēṭṭaicey moyyiruḷvāy | vaḻaṅkā vatariṉ vaḻaṅkeṉṟu mōviṉṟem vaḷḷalaiyē ||

Cf. IAC17, p. 135: aḵtāmāṟu: talaimakaṉ iravukkuṟivantu oḻukāniṉṟa kālattu orunāḷ talaimakaṉ collāmē avaṉāṟ ceyyappaṭuṅ kuṟippukkaḷ tāmē veḷippaṭṭaṉa. avai puṉṉaikkāy nīriliṭutalum, puḷḷeḻupputalumeṉa ivai.

Cf. AN68.1–14: aṉṉāy vāḻivēṇ ṭaṉṉainam paṭappait | taṇṇayat tamaṉṟa kūtaḷaṅ kuḻaiya | viṉṉicai yaruvip pāṭu meṉatūuṅ | kēṭṭiyō vāḻivēṇ ṭaṉṉainam paṭappai | yūṭṭi yaṉṉa voṇṭaḷirac ceyalai | yōṅkuciṉait toṭutta vūcal pāmpeṉa | muḻumuta ṟumiya vurumeṟin taṉṟē | yiṉṉuṅ kēṭṭiyō veṉavumaḵ taṟiyā | ḷaṉṉaiyuṅ kaṉaituyiṉ maṭintaṉa ḷataṉṟalai | muṉṉuyir maṭintaṉṟāṟ poḻutē kātalar | varuva rāyiṟ paruva mituveṉac | cuṭarntilaṅ kelvaḷai nekiḻnta namvayiṟ | paṭarnta vuḷḷam paḻutaṉ ṟāka | vantaṉar vāḻi tōḻi
Cf. IAC16, p. 134: tāytuñcāmaiyeṉpatu talaimakaṉ iravukkuṟivantu oḻukāniṉṟa kālattu orunāḷ tāy kaṇpaṭāḷāki makaḷai aṟivum ācāramuṅ kaṟpittaṟporuṭṭāka irukkum; iruntakālattum iṭaiyīṭāmeṉpatu.

Though C1’s reading is understandable, and one could argue that it should be chosen on the principle of lectio difficilior, I have opted for KKms, as I believe UVC did. There are nine occurrences of vēl (‘spear’) in the TNV poems. In six of them (not counting this example), it is followed by aṇṇal (‘majesty’) and in the two other cases, it is followed by viṭalai (‘young warrior’). In every instance then, it is a property of a young man, and it never functions as an aṉmoḻittokai (an exocentric, or bahuvrīhi, compound). I follow the pattern of the text that is supported by KKms, even though I accept that this reading might have been a result of normalising the less common, and slightly more difficult to understand eṭuttalum (‘to raise’) found in C1. Were one to read that, the second half of the poem would translate as: ‘And by raising [his] long spear with a shining leaf-tip, he has come to the meeting-place to make our lonely misery go away.’ The repetition of eṭuttal reads inelegantly, as does the lack of an explicit subject. I cannot explain how this corruption would have occurred in C1, but I still regard the overwhelming weight of evidence from the TNV to support reading aṇṇal.
Cf. PK167.2–4 (IAC18, p. 148): vañcippaim pūmpuṟaviṟ | pūḻip puṟamaññai yaṉṉanal lāykoḷkam pōtutiyēṟ | ṟāḻik kuvaḷainiṉ kaṇpōl viriyun taṭamalarē ||
Cf. PK168.3–4 (IAC18, p. 148): vaḷaikkoṉṟu kaimmaṅkai yāyceṉṟu kōṭuniṉ vāyuḷvantu | muḷaikkiṉṟa muḷḷeyiṟ ṟērkoṇ ṭarumpiṉa mullaikaḷē ||
Cf. IAC18, p. 147: ivvāṟu talaimakaṉ varavu uṇarntu, tōḻi kuvaḷai yalarntaṉavēṟ kāṇpām, paranta mullai arumpiṉavēṟ kāṇpāmeṉac collit talaimakaḷaik koṇṭupōtum.
Cf. TK163.2–4: kaṇkaṭanta | vintī varamivai kāṇiṉ ṉiruḷcēr kuḻaṟkeḻilcēr | cantī varamuṟi yumveṟi vīyun tarukuvaṉē ||

The parallel between the first line of this poem and the final line of PK 167 is too close to ignore. This edition’s reading, following UVC and supported by KKms – niṉ kaṇ pōl – is identical to the PK, where it is explicit that the water lilies are like her eyes. Likewise in PK 168, it is explicit that jasmine blossoms are like the teeth in her mouth – niṉ vāyuḷ. This seems to be a pattern in this poem archetype.
Cf. PK139.3–4 (IAC17, p. 136): iṟaivā yaṇivaḷai yāyeṉṉai kollō viraviṉellān | tuṟaivā yiḷampuṉṉai mēlaṉṉa moṉṟun tuyiṉṟilavē ||
Cf. PK140.3–4 (IAC17, p. 136): iṉṟami ḻaṉṉanal lāynampaiṅ kāṉaliṉvāyt | tūniṉṟa meṉciṟai yaṉṉamiṉ ṟeṉṟun tuyiṉṟilavē ||
Cf. TK172.2–4: eṉṉaṅ kalamara veytiya tōveḻiṉ muttantottip | poṉṉaṅ kalarpuṉṉaic cēkkaiyiṉ vāyppulam puṟṟumuṟṟum | aṉṉam pularu maḷavun tuyilā taḻuṅkiṉavē ||
Cf. KT128.4–5 (IAC17, p. 137): cēya ḷariyōṭ paṭarti | nōyai neñcē nōyppā lōyē ||
